newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Once mighty Korzhakov victim of Kremlin intrigue.
newsitem.headline: Once mighty Korzhakov victim of Kremlin intrigue.

text.p: Alexander Korzhakov, facing dismissal from the Russian army after being accused of telling "lies" about President Boris Yeltsin and his family, has fallen victim to the very Kremlin intrigues he once championed.

The sacking completes a dramatic fall from grace for Yeltsin's former bodyguard, tennis, swimming and -- some say -- drinking partner who once counted the president as a close personal friend and controlled access to him.

The pugnacious Korzhakov, ousted from the Kremlin in a purge of policy hawks in June, recently accused presidential chief of staff Anatoly Chubais of trying to seize real power and said Yeltsin's daughter Tatyana was in league with him.
Korzhakov, 46, has also hinted he is ready to disclose confidential, and potentially explosive, information gained during more than a decade at Yeltsin's side.

"After his sacking on June 20, 1996, Lieutenant-General Alexander Korzhakov has come out with a series of lies concerning the Russian president and members of his family," said an order released by Yeltsin's press office on Monday.
The statement said Yeltsin had ordered his security service to prepare the paperwork for sacking Korzhakov from the army but did not say if he would be stripped of his military rank.
The order was released as Korzhakov, who stood by Yeltsin for 11 years, prepared to launch a political career of his own in a parliamentary by-election in the central region of Tula.
The position became available after Yeltsin named Alexander Lebed, who held it, his national security chief in July. The outspoken Lebed was recently sacked for insubordination.

The burly ex-KGB general appears to have formed an alliance with Lebed, who he says has the "best political future in the country". They also share a dislike for Chubais, who Korzhakov says is trying to establish his own "regency".

Korzhakov has gone on the offensive after years in the shadows but has also been attacked himself. He is fighting allegations by a former top businessman that he made a multi-million-dollar extortion demand.

Korzhakov had for some time shown signs of uneasiness at losing ground to liberals in Yeltsin's camp. As Russia's presidential election heated up in May, Korzhakov caused outrage by saying the poll should be put off to avert unrest.
Korzhakov told the German magazine Der Spiegel that he had called for the election to be postponed because he feared for the president's health.
"We could see clearly how exhausted Yeltsin was and that he might not survive a demanding election campaign," he said in an interview published on Monday.
"The doctors treating him told me in writing as early as May 20 about the danger. Their warning sounded dramatic: The president can only work for a few hours a day."
Asked why he had never made this letter public, Korzhakov accused Yeltsin's daughter Tatyana of controlling the flow of information to the president.
Korzhakov had been close to the Kremlin leader since he was assigned to be his bodyguard in 1985 when Yeltsin was Moscow Communist Party boss.

When Yeltsin was hounded out of office by former Soviet president Mikhail Gorbachev in 1987, Korzhakov defied KGB tradition by standing by his old boss, even driving him around in his own modest Zhiguli car.

The wheel of history turned in Yeltsin's favour and Korzhakov went with him. When Yeltsin clambered atop a tank outside the White House to defy a hardline coup attempt against Gorbachev in August 1991, Korzhakov stood behind him.
After Yeltsin moved into the Kremlin he put his old friend in charge of his personal security apparatus and from then on Korzhakov was constantly at his side.
But by 1994 it was clear he enjoyed influence which extended far beyond his job of organising Yeltsin's security detail and opening the door of his boss's limousine.

Reports of him being a Kremlin "grey eminence" with an unusually broad portfolio emerged that year when he denounced World Bank proposals to reform Russia's oil export system in a letter addressed to Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin.
The letter prompted Izvestia newspaper to ask: "Who is running the country -- Yeltsin, Chernomyrdin or General Korzhakov?"
